question_text: An FM integration unexpectedly returns incomplete or truncated responses. Context window diagnostic logs show inputs near the model's maximum token limit. Which remediation approaches are correct? (Choose TWO)

options.text: Use dynamic chunking to limit conversation history size passed to the FM
Redesign the prompt to use summarised conversation history rather than full raw history
Increase the max output tokens to compensate for input truncation
Use a larger FM so it has more parameters to handle long inputs
Add more detail to the system prompt to guide the FM on long inputs

explanation: Skill 5.2.1 describes context window overflow diagnostics, dynamic chunking strategies, and prompt design optimisation. (A) Dynamic chunking limits how many history tokens are included in the context window at any time. (B) Summarising conversation history compresses many tokens of history into a small summary, freeing context space. Increasing max output tokens doesn't affect the input token limit. A larger FM doesn't have a larger context window by default. Adding more to the system prompt worsens the overflow.
source_topic: Context window, truncation, dynamic chunking

question_text: A Lambda function calling Bedrock frequently returns `ValidationException: Input is too long for requested model`. What is the correct debugging workflow?

options.text: Increase Lambda memory
Log the input token count before each API call, identify which inputs exceed the model's context limit, and apply input truncation or chunking
Ignore the error — it is intermittent and will self-resolve
Switch to a different AWS region where the limit may be higher

explanation: Skill 5.2.2 describes error logging and request validation for FM integration issues. The correct approach is: instrument the input with a token counter, log it to CloudWatch, identify inputs that breach the model limit, and apply remediation (truncation, summarisation, chunking). Lambda memory doesn't affect the FM's token limit. ValidationException errors are deterministic — they won't self-resolve without code changes. The context limit is a model property, not a region configuration.
source_topic: FM API errors, ValidationException, token limit

question_text: FM responses to a customer-facing assistant have degraded — answers are suddenly verbose and off-topic. The application code has not changed. A new prompt template was deployed yesterday. Which debugging approach is most systematic?

options.text: Roll back the entire application to last month's deployment
Use Bedrock Prompt Management version comparison — A/B test the previous and new prompt templates against a golden question set and compare output quality metrics
Increase FM temperature to generate more varied responses
Switch to a different FM provider

explanation: Skill 5.2.3 describes prompt testing frameworks and version comparison for prompt engineering issues. Bedrock Prompt Management retains versioned templates; comparing the current version against the previous one on a golden question set isolates the prompt change as the root cause. Rolling back the full application is overly broad and loses new features. Increasing temperature worsens inconsistency. Switching FM providers doesn't fix a prompt regression.
source_topic: Prompt versioning, A/B testing, Bedrock Prompt Management

question_text: Users report that the RAG assistant gives correct answers to some questions but completely ignores relevant documents for others. How should the team diagnose the retrieval failure?

options.text: Assume the FM is hallucinating and increase the top-k retrieval count

Inspect retrieval logs: check embedding quality for failing queries, examine cosine similarity scores for retrieved chunks, and verify that relevant documents are present and properly chunked in the index
Switch to a larger FM — retrieval issues are always generation problems
Delete and rebuild the knowledge base from scratch

explanation: Skill 5.2.4 describes retrieval system troubleshooting including embedding quality diagnostics, drift monitoring, and vectorisation issue resolution. The correct systematic approach: check if relevant documents exist in the index; verify their chunks are appropriately sized; inspect similarity scores for failing queries (low scores indicate embedding mismatch); check for embedding quality drift if a model was recently updated. Increasing top-k may mask the problem. Retrieval failures are distinct from generation — switching FM won't fix a missing-document issue. Full rebuilds are disruptive and don't diagnose root cause.
source_topic: Retrieval debugging, embedding quality, chunking

topic: Prompt maintenance with CloudWatch and X-Ray
question_text: A production FM assistant started producing inconsistent responses after a prompt template variable was added. The CloudWatch Logs show some prompts fail schema validation. Which tools and approach diagnose and fix the issue? (Choose TWO)

options.text: Use CloudWatch Logs Insights to query prompt invocation logs and identify which template variable substitutions are missing or malformed
Use AWS X-Ray to trace the prompt construction path through the application and identify where variables are missing
Increase Lambda memory to resolve template substitution failures
Use Amazon Rekognition to detect problems in prompt text
Use Amazon Macie to scan prompts for PII causing failures

explanation: Skill 5.2.5 explicitly cites CloudWatch Logs to diagnose prompt confusion and X-Ray to implement prompt observability pipelines, alongside schema validation for format inconsistencies. (A) CloudWatch Logs Insights can filter invocations where variable substitution was incomplete — showing the malformed prompt. (B) X-Ray traces the full request path, pinpointing which Lambda function or step lost the variable value. Lambda memory has no effect on template logic. Rekognition is for image/video. Macie detects PII, not template syntax errors.
source_topic: CloudWatch Logs Insights, X-Ray, prompt observability

topic: Embedding model version drift — RAG silent failure
question_text: A financial services RAG application worked correctly for months. After a Lambda code update, it returns 'no relevant information found' for queries that previously retrieved accurate results. CloudWatch shows no errors, X-Ray confirms successful FM invocations, and OpenSearch is healthy with no index changes. What is the most likely root cause?

options.text: The Lambda IAM role is missing bedrock:InvokeModel permission
The FM temperature was inadvertently increased in the code update
The document vectors in OpenSearch were deleted during the deployment
The Lambda code update switched to a different embedding model version, creating a vector-space mismatch with the existing index

explanation: Skill 5.2.4 (retrieval system troubleshooting) describes embedding model version drift as a classic silent RAG failure. If the Lambda now embeds queries using model v2 while the OpenSearch index contains vectors from model v1, the two vector spaces are mathematically incompatible — no vectors match, retrieval returns zero results. The key diagnostic clue is 'silent failure': no errors (IAM permission errors produce AccessDeniedException logs; deleted indices produce empty-results warnings with different signatures). The FM temperature (B) only affects generation step 2 — retrieval failure happens in step 1 before generation. Vector deletion (C) would normally produce warnings.
source_topic: Embedding drift, vector-space mismatch, RAG troubleshooting

topic: KB ingestion logging for document-level failures
question_text: A company ingests 2,000 documents per day into a Bedrock Knowledge Base from S3. Some documents fail silently — they appear processed but queries return no results for their content. The team needs to identify which specific documents failed and why. Which solution provides document-level ingestion diagnostics?

options.text: Enable Knowledge Base logging to CloudWatch Logs; use CloudWatch Logs Insights to query per-document status codes (SUCCESS / EMBEDDING_FAILED / INDEXING_FAILED)
Enable AWS CloudTrail data events for all Bedrock APIs
Enable Bedrock Model Invocation Logging to capture embedding metrics
Use Amazon CloudWatch Application Signals to detect KB performance issues

explanation: Skill 5.2.4 and 4.3.2 describe Knowledge Base logging for ingestion troubleshooting. The KB-specific logging feature emits per-document status records to CloudWatch Logs (RESOURCE_IGNORED, EMBEDDING_FAILED, INDEXING_FAILED, SUCCESS) that can be queried with Logs Insights. CloudTrail (B) records which IAM principal called StartIngestionJob — it has no visibility into per-document processing outcomes. Bedrock Model Invocation Logging (C) captures prompt/response content during chat inference — unrelated to the background ingestion process. CloudWatch Application Signals (D) is APM for microservices (EKS/API Gateway latency) — not for KB ingestion diagnostics.
source_topic: Bedrock Knowledge Base logging, CloudWatch Logs Insights

question_text: During a high-traffic product launch, a Bedrock-powered chatbot begins returning ThrottlingException errors. The on-call engineer needs to resolve the issue quickly. Which combination of actions is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Implement exponential backoff with jitter in the client so retries do not cause a retry storm
Purchase Provisioned Throughput for the model to guarantee sustained invocation capacity
Reduce the model temperature to stop throttling
Switch to a larger context window size to avoid the quota
Disable all guardrails to reduce latency overhead

explanation: ThrottlingException indicates the invocation rate has exceeded the on-demand quota. Exponential backoff with jitter (option A) is the standard immediate mitigation — it spreads retries over time and prevents a retry storm. Provisioned Throughput (option B) is the long-term fix: it reserves dedicated model capacity ensuring sustained throughput. Lowering temperature, using a larger context window, or disabling guardrails do not affect throttling quotas.
source_topic: Throttling, Provisioned Throughput, exponential backoff, quota management

topic: Amazon Polly — text-to-speech in GenAI pipeline
question_text: A GenAI virtual assistant generates text responses. The team wants to add voice output so users can listen to answers on a mobile app. Which AWS service converts the FM-generated text to natural-sounding speech?

options.text: Amazon Polly — converts text to lifelike speech, supporting multiple languages and neural voices
Amazon Transcribe — converts speech to text (the opposite direction)
Amazon Lex — builds conversational interfaces but does not output audio directly
Amazon Rekognition — analyzes audio and video content

explanation: Amazon Polly is AWS's text-to-speech service, producing lifelike audio from text in dozens of languages using standard and neural voices. Transcribe is speech-to-text (the reverse). Lex builds conversational AI chatbots and does use Polly under the hood, but Lex itself is not directly invoked for text-to-speech synthesis in a custom pipeline. Rekognition analyzes visual media — not audio synthesis.
source_topic: Amazon Polly, text-to-speech, GenAI voice interface

topic: Amazon Athena — querying S3 data lakes for GenAI evaluation
question_text: A team stores FM invocation logs and evaluation metrics in Amazon S3 in Parquet format. They want to run ad-hoc SQL queries against this data to identify patterns in hallucinations and latency spikes without loading data into a database. Which service enables serverless SQL directly on S3?

options.text: Amazon Athena — runs serverless SQL queries directly on S3 data using standard SQL, with no data movement or ETL
Amazon Redshift — requires loading data into a managed warehouse first
Amazon DynamoDB — a NoSQL key-value store that does not support SQL
Amazon RDS — a relational database requiring data migration from S3

explanation: Amazon Athena is a serverless interactive query service that runs SQL directly on data in S3 (Parquet, CSV, JSON, ORC, etc.) with no ETL or data loading required. This is ideal for ad-hoc analysis of FM invocation logs. Redshift requires loading data into a warehouse. DynamoDB is NoSQL. RDS requires migration from S3.
source_topic: Amazon Athena, serverless SQL on S3, GenAI observability

topic: Amazon QuickSight — BI dashboards for GenAI metrics
question_text: A GenAI platform team wants to build visual dashboards showing token usage trends, cost per team, and guardrail trigger rates over time, accessible to non-technical stakeholders. Which AWS service is purpose-built for this?

options.text: Amazon QuickSight — a serverless BI service for building interactive dashboards from AWS data sources including Athena, S3, and CloudWatch
Amazon CloudWatch — provides metrics and alarms but is not a BI dashboarding tool for business stakeholders
AWS Cost Explorer — shows cost trends but cannot be customized for GenAI-specific metrics like guardrail triggers
Amazon SageMaker Studio — a development IDE, not a BI dashboard platform

explanation: Amazon QuickSight is AWS's managed BI service, enabling rich visual dashboards for business stakeholders with no infrastructure to manage. It connects to Athena, S3, CloudWatch, RDS, and more, making it suitable for GenAI usage analytics. CloudWatch is operational monitoring (not stakeholder-facing BI). Cost Explorer is limited to billing dimensions. SageMaker Studio is a data science IDE.
source_topic: Amazon QuickSight, BI dashboards, GenAI metrics visualization

question_text: A Bedrock application starts returning errors 'Input is too long' during peak usage. Analysis shows the conversation history is growing indefinitely with each turn. What is the CORRECT fix?

options.text: Switch to a model with a larger context window

Implement a Lambda function that counts tokens (using CountTokens API), and if the total prompt exceeds 80% of the context limit, prunes the oldest conversation turns or summarises the history before sending
Increase Lambda memory to handle larger inputs
Enable Bedrock Guardrails to truncate inputs automatically

explanation: The root cause is unbounded conversation history growing beyond the context window. The fix is proactive context management: use the CountTokens API to estimate total prompt size, and if it approaches the limit, prune oldest turns or summarise the history. Switching to a larger context window model (A) only delays the problem. Lambda memory has no effect on FM context limits. Guardrails filter content for safety — they don't manage context window sizing.
source_topic: Context window management: CountTokens + history pruning

question_text: A RAG chatbot gives accurate answers to recent questions but increasingly poor answers to questions about older documents. Investigation shows newer documents were added to the knowledge base after a Titan Embeddings model version upgrade. What is the likely root cause?

options.text: The older documents have expired from the vector store via TTL
Embedding model version mismatch: older documents were embedded with the previous model version, newer with the new version — vectors in different semantic spaces cannot be accurately compared
The context window is too small to handle older, longer documents
The knowledge base needs more shards to accommodate more documents

explanation: Embedding version mismatch is the classic silent failure mode: older documents were embedded with Titan Embeddings v1, newer documents with v2. Since both versions produce vectors in different semantic spaces, similarity comparisons between a v2 query vector and v1 document vectors are inaccurate — causing poor retrieval for old documents. Fix: re-embed ALL documents with the current model version and rebuild the index. TTL doesn't apply here. Context window size affects generation, not retrieval.
source_topic: Embedding model version mismatch causing silent retrieval failure

question_text: A developer's Bedrock application is generating inconsistent output formats — sometimes JSON, sometimes plain text, despite a system prompt saying 'Output in JSON'. The developer wants to debug which exact prompt is being sent to the model including all variables substituted. Where is this information accessible?

options.text: AWS CloudTrail — records the InvokeModel API call metadata
Bedrock Model Invocation Logs (ModelInvocationInput trace) — captures the exact finalised prompt sent to the model for each invocation
AWS Config — tracks system prompt configuration changes
Amazon Macie — scans model inputs for sensitive data

explanation: Bedrock Model Invocation Logs, specifically the ModelInvocationInput trace, captures the EXACT prompt that was sent to the model — including all variable substitutions, conversation history, and system prompts. This allows developers to verify what the model actually received vs. what they intended. CloudTrail records API metadata but not the full prompt body. Config tracks resource configurations. Macie scans S3 for sensitive data.
source_topic: Bedrock ModelInvocationInput trace for exact prompt debugging

question_text: A team uses parameterised Bedrock prompts (with {tone}, {language}, {text} variables). Some combinations of variables cause the model to produce confused or irrelevant outputs. How should the team systematically identify which variable combinations are problematic?

options.text: Deploy to production and wait for user complaints
Create a test matrix of all variable combinations and run Bedrock evaluation jobs against all combinations, reviewing outputs for confusion patterns
Remove all variables from the prompt template
Use CloudWatch Logs Insights to query for responses containing the word 'confused'

explanation: Systematic prompt debugging for parameterised templates requires testing all relevant variable combinations — a test matrix approach. Bedrock evaluation jobs can run all combinations against an evaluation rubric and flag problematic outputs. This identifies the specific combinations that fail before deployment. Waiting for user complaints (A) is reactive. Removing variables defeats the template purpose. CloudWatch queries (D) only catch a specific symptom and only after deployment.
source_topic: Template testing: variable combination test matrix for parameterised prompts

question_text: A RAG system returns technically correct chunks but users still receive incomplete answers. Investigation reveals the retrieved chunks break in the middle of important concepts (e.g., a legal clause split across two chunks). What is the root cause and fix?

options.text: The FM has a hallucination problem — fine-tune the model
Fixed-size chunking is splitting at character boundaries rather than semantic boundaries — switch to semantic/hierarchical chunking to preserve concept integrity
The vector store is returning stale embeddings — rebuild the index
Increase k (number of retrieved chunks) from 5 to 20

explanation: When chunks break in the middle of concepts (clauses, sentences, logical units), the root cause is chunking strategy — typically fixed-size chunking at character/token boundaries. The fix is semantic/recursive chunking that splits at natural boundaries (sentences, paragraphs, section headings) preserving concept integrity. Hierarchical chunking (small for retrieval, larger parent for context) is also effective. This is a chunking strategy issue, not a model hallucination or staleness problem. Increasing k just adds more partially-broken chunks.
source_topic: Chunking boundary issues — semantic chunking to fix incomplete answers

question_text: A Lambda function calling Bedrock suddenly starts failing with ThrottlingException after a new feature release doubled traffic. The errors are intermittent. What is the CORRECT handling approach (ordered from first to last attempt)?

options.text: Immediately purchase Provisioned Throughput and disable retries
(1) Implement exponential backoff with jitter retries in Lambda, (2) add SQS buffer to absorb traffic spikes, (3) if persistent, purchase Provisioned Throughput
Switch to a different model that has more available capacity
Increase Lambda concurrency to 10,000 to process faster

explanation: The graduated approach: (1) Exponential backoff handles transient throttling from spiky traffic — most cases resolve without additional infrastructure. (2) SQS buffer decouples request intake from processing, absorbing traffic spikes gracefully. (3) Provisioned Throughput is the solution only if throttling persists despite buffering, indicating sustained capacity need. Immediately purchasing Provisioned Throughput is costly if backoff + buffering resolves it. Switching models may degrade quality. More Lambda concurrency increases the rate of throttled requests.
source_topic: ThrottlingException: backoff → SQS buffer → Provisioned Throughput

question_text: A developer notices that Bedrock responses seem to 'forget' information from the beginning of very long conversations. The conversation history is 8,000 tokens and the model's context window is 8,192 tokens. What is happening and how should it be fixed?

options.text: The model has a memory bug — contact AWS Support
The conversation is silently truncated at the token limit — early context is dropped. Fix: implement sliding window (keep last N turns) or periodic summarisation to compress old history
The FM temperature is too high causing inconsistent recall
DynamoDB TTL is expiring the conversation history prematurely

explanation: When a prompt approaches the context window limit, the model (or the API client) silently truncates the oldest content to fit. This causes the model to 'forget' early conversation context. Fix: implement a sliding window that retains only the most recent N turns, or use a Lambda to periodically summarise old history into a compressed paragraph — preserving key information in fewer tokens. This is not a model bug, temperature issue, or TTL problem.
source_topic: Silent context truncation — sliding window or history summarisation

question_text: A Bedrock streaming application (using InvokeModelWithResponseStream) intermittently stops streaming mid-response with no error returned — the connection just closes. What are the MOST likely causes?

options.text: Lambda function timeout reached before streaming completed — increase Lambda timeout or switch to shorter responses
API Gateway WebSocket connection timeout — API Gateway WebSocket connections time out after 10 minutes by default
The model has a bias problem causing early termination
Bedrock Guardrails blocked the streaming response mid-generation
The FM reached the max_tokens limit and terminated generation normally

explanation: (A) Lambda has a 15-minute maximum timeout. If streaming takes longer than the configured timeout (often 30 seconds default), the function terminates mid-stream with no error. (B) API Gateway WebSocket connections have a 10-minute idle and connection timeout — long streaming responses may exceed this. Both can cause silent mid-stream closure. Model bias (C) doesn't cause connection closure. Guardrails (D) produce a guardrail intervention response, not a silent close. max_tokens termination (E) sends a completion event, not a connection drop.
source_topic: Streaming interruption: Lambda timeout + API Gateway WebSocket timeout

topic: KB ingestion logging for document-level failures
question_text: A team runs a Bedrock Knowledge Base ingestion job and notices some documents were not embedded. The job completed without a global error. How should they diagnose which specific documents failed and why?

options.text: Check AWS CloudTrail for the CreateIngestionJob API call errors
Query CloudWatch Logs for the ingestion job — Bedrock logs document-level errors including which files failed and the error reason
Use Amazon Macie to scan the S3 source bucket for corrupted files
Re-run the entire ingestion job and check if the count changes

explanation: Bedrock Knowledge Base ingestion jobs log document-level processing details (including individual file failures and error reasons) to CloudWatch Logs. This is the primary troubleshooting resource for identifying which specific documents failed during ingestion. CloudTrail records the API call metadata but not per-document processing errors. Macie discovers sensitive data, not ingestion errors. Re-running without diagnosis wastes time and may not change the outcome if the root cause (e.g., malformed PDFs) is not fixed.
source_topic: CloudWatch Logs for Bedrock KB document-level ingestion errors

topic: Prompt maintenance with CloudWatch and X-Ray
question_text: A team wants to trace exactly which version of a parameterised prompt was used for a specific production request that generated a problematic response. How can they correlate the prompt version to the specific request?

options.text: Check the Bedrock console for recent invocations
Use AWS X-Ray with custom annotations logging the prompt_version_id alongside the trace; then query X-Ray for the specific request trace
Check CloudWatch Metrics for the prompt version usage count
Use Amazon Macie to trace the prompt content

explanation: AWS X-Ray traces can be annotated with custom key-value metadata (annotations) like prompt_version_id. When investigating a specific problematic request, you query X-Ray for the trace ID of that request and see which prompt version was used. This enables prompt version attribution for debugging. The Bedrock console shows recent invocations but not per-request prompt version metadata. CloudWatch Metrics shows aggregate counts. Macie scans data at rest.
source_topic: X-Ray custom annotations for prompt version tracing

question_text: A RAG knowledge base was working well for 3 months. Then the company updated its document corpus (replaced old versions with new versions). Now the system returns a mix of old and new information, causing conflicting answers. What maintenance task was likely missed?

options.text: The fine-tuned model needs retraining on new documents
Old document vectors were not deleted from the knowledge base when old files were replaced — stale vectors must be deleted and a re-ingestion run
The Lambda function has a bug returning cached old responses
Bedrock Guardrails are blocking new document content

explanation: When documents are replaced, the old vectors remain in the knowledge base unless explicitly deleted. The knowledge base now contains both old and new embeddings for the same topics, causing retrieval to return conflicting information. Fix: (1) identify old document IDs in the vector store, (2) delete their vectors, (3) re-trigger ingestion for the new document versions. This is a data maintenance issue, not a model, Lambda, or Guardrails issue.
source_topic: Stale vector cleanup when documents are replaced in KB

question_text: A team migrates from calling a Bedrock model directly (model ID hardcoded) to using Bedrock cross-region inference. After migration, all requests receive AccessDeniedException. What is the MOST likely cause?

options.text: The model is not available in the destination region
The IAM role lacks bedrock:InvokeModel permission for the cross-region inference profile ARN — cross-region inference uses a different ARN format than direct model invocations
Bedrock Guardrails are blocking cross-region requests
The Lambda timeout is too short for cross-region calls

explanation: Cross-region inference in Bedrock uses inference profile ARNs (format: arn:aws:bedrock:us-east-1::inference-profile/...) rather than direct model ARNs. When migrating from direct invocation, the IAM policy must be updated to grant bedrock:InvokeModel permission for the inference profile ARN — not just the model ARN. This is a common migration pitfall. Regional availability issues would produce a different error. Guardrails don't block cross-region calls. Lambda timeout causes TaskTimedOut, not AccessDeniedException.
source_topic: Cross-region inference IAM: inference profile ARN vs model ARN

question_text: A developer wants to test whether their OpenSearch vector index is working correctly after recent changes. They embed a known phrase ('customer return policy') and search for it — expecting to find the exact document they know contains that phrase. Which diagnostic step confirms the vector index is correctly matching semantically related content?

options.text: Check the OpenSearch cluster's FreeStorageSpace metric in CloudWatch
Embed the known phrase and call the Bedrock Retrieve API (or OpenSearch k-NN search directly) — verify the known document ranks in the top results
Review CloudTrail logs for recent OpenSearch API calls
Run a SQL SELECT query on the OpenSearch index

explanation: The correct diagnostic is to embed a known phrase and run a vector similarity search — then verify that the document known to contain that phrase appears in the top results. If it doesn't, the embedding pipeline, chunking, or index has a problem. FreeStorageSpace indicates storage health, not retrieval accuracy. CloudTrail shows API calls, not search quality. OpenSearch uses a query DSL, not SQL SELECT.
source_topic: Vector index diagnostic: embed known phrase, verify top-k results

question_text: A team updates a production system prompt but forgets to update the version tracking in Bedrock Prompt Management. In production, different Lambda instances are using different prompt versions (old cache vs. new). How should this race condition be prevented in future deployments?

options.text: Use Lambda reserved concurrency = 1 so only one instance runs at a time
Store the canonical prompt version ID in AWS AppConfig and update it atomically; Lambda reads from AppConfig on each invocation — ensuring consistent version usage
Redeploy all Lambda functions simultaneously whenever the prompt changes
Increase Lambda timeout to ensure old cache expires before new requests come in

explanation: AWS AppConfig provides atomic configuration updates with built-in cache invalidation. Lambda functions read the active prompt version ID from AppConfig on each request (using the AppConfig Lambda extension's cache with a configurable TTL). When the prompt is updated in AppConfig, all Lambda instances pick up the new version within the TTL window — no redeployment needed, no race condition. Lambda concurrency = 1 eliminates parallelism. Redeploying all Lambda functions simultaneously has a blue/green complexity. Timeout adjustments don't address version consistency.
source_topic: AppConfig for atomic prompt version updates across Lambda instances
